name: Capture the incident timeline and communications contemporaneously
description: Record detection, containment, and closure timestamps, actions taken, and communications issued as the response happens, rather than reconstructing a narrative after closure.

steps.action: Adopt an incident record template with required timeline fields, so capture is prompted rather than remembered.
Open the incident record at declaration and update it during the response, not at closure.
Link the working channel or bridge to the record so the contemporaneous trail is preserved and reconcilable.
Record each communication issued with recipient, content summary, and time.
Measure containment and communication elapsed time against the committed timeframes and report on it.
Assign a scribe role for higher-severity incidents so record-keeping does not compete with response.

implementation_considerations: Nobody updates a form mid-incident unless it is trivially fast. A pinned channel and a scribe outperform a detailed template every time.
Linking the working channel is usually more valuable than any structured field, because it is genuinely contemporaneous.
Set committed timeframes from what past incidents actually achieved, or the record will simply document breaches.
typical_duration: Days to set up; proven on the next incident.
prerequisites: An incident management or ticketing system used as the record

verification_method.how: For an incident after the change, confirm the record carries detection, containment, and closure timestamps, actions with actors, and communications issued, with creation timestamps contemporaneous with the response.

residual_risk_note: A good record demonstrates how the response ran; it does not make the response faster or better.
period_limitation_note: Records for incidents already closed cannot be reconstructed into contemporaneous evidence. Backfilling produces a narrative and auditors read it as one.
notes: Addresses an insufficient-evidence observation: the response may have been handled well, but it cannot be demonstrated.
